name: ABL Landscape Architecture
description: ABL Landscape Architecture is an award-winning, client-focused landscape architecture firm based in Lexington, Virginia offering expertise in institutional, civic, residential and commercial landscape architecture projects.
statement: ABL Landscape Architecture is principally devoted to the adaptation of historic, environmentally sensitive landscapes to contemporary needs and goals.

intro: The firm seeks to distill the essence of a site, and to respond to its innate character and context with creative, enduring design. ABL assists clients through all phases from initial concept to landscape establishment and maturation. We embrace open dialogue and exploration with clients, allied professionals, contractors, and end-users.

Mindful of the client's need to visualize the final product and also of the client's cost constraints in landscape construction and maintenance, ABL seeks every reasonable means to narrow the uncertainty between design incubation and the desired outcome. Such techniques include photo simulation, 3D scale models, material samples, full scale mock-ups, detailed review of pricing, dialogue with both grounds staff and end-users, and frequent site visits.
studio.note: ABL is a SWaM certified small business.

process.lead: ABL carries a project from research into the history of its site, through design in dialogue with the client, to construction and the establishment of the landscape.

sections.title: Research
text: Design begins with research. ABL studies how a site came to its present form, what it was intended to be, and how it has since been altered, and takes that record as the basis of its design. At Courthouse Square in Lexington the research reached back to the act of 1777, which fixed the county court on the first Tuesday of each month, and to Court Day, when families from the outlying farms came to town to trade and to hear the news. The premise of the design, that the square is first a place of assembly, came from that history.

In Lexington and Rockbridge County the firm works from long familiarity with the place. Its principal, Arthur Bartenstein, is president of the Rockbridge Historical Society and serves on the City of Lexington's Architectural Review Board and Tree Committee.

quote.text: Registered in terms of place, but also registered in terms of time.

sections.title: Dialogue
text: ABL treats design as a dialogue among the client, the site and the design team. The client's intentions are tested against the site, which determines part of the answer, and the design develops as that exchange continues. On campus and civic projects the dialogue extends to architects, engineers and the staff who will maintain the grounds, and proposals are brought to them while they can still change.

sections.title: Models and mock-ups
text: Clients are asked to approve, and to fund, places they cannot yet see. ABL therefore seeks every reasonable means to narrow the uncertainty between a design and its result: proposals are studied in sketches, photo simulations and scale models, materials are reviewed as samples, pricing is examined in detail, and before construction the design is mocked up at full scale on the site.

sections.title: Construction and establishment
text: ABL remains with a project through construction and the establishment of the landscape. It has worked with many of the region's contractors for decades and visits the site frequently while work is under way. Planting is specified by staff who know which plants do well in this ground, among them a certified arborist with eighteen years' experience in landscape installation and maintenance.

intro: ABL provides master planning, landscape architecture, cultural landscape reports, feasibility studies and planting design for campuses, civic spaces and historic properties.
For private properties the firm is engaged for a consultation, a planting plan, a master plan, or the design of a single element such as a stair.

work.intro: Campus, civic and preservation projects in Lexington, Rockbridge County and elsewhere in Virginia: built work, shown with the plans and studies that precede it.
